claims.title: Unbounded memory allocation in AMQP binary deserialization
claims.impact: Denial of Service: attacker can send AMQP message with oversized length-prefix to cause OutOfMemoryError, crashing the client or server.
claims.evidence: readBytes() allocates byte[contentLength] where contentLength is read from untrusted AMQP wire protocol (line 86). The check at line 87 allows allocation up to Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 bytes (~2.1 GB). Called recursively from readLongstr(), readTable(), readArray() via readFieldValue().

claims.title: Integer overflow in timestamp deserialization
claims.impact: An attacker sending an AMQP message with an extreme timestamp value (e.g., Long.MAX_VALUE) can cause the multiplication to overflow, resulting in a Date object with an incorrect timestamp. This could affect any application logic that depends on correct message timestamps for TTL calculation, message ordering, or validity checks.
claims.evidence: Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);` Multiplies a long value read directly from the untrusted network stream by 1000 without overflow checking. When the long value exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 (~9.22e18), the multiplication overflows, producing incorrect timestamps.

claims.title: Unbounded recursion depth in AMQP field value deserialization
claims.impact: Denial of Service: attacker can cause StackOverflowError by crafting deeply nested AMQP table or array structures, crashing the client.
claims.evidence: readFieldValue() is recursive. Case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable(), which calls readFieldValue() in a while loop (line 150). Case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray(), which calls readFieldValue() in a while loop (line 245). No recursion depth counter or maximum nesting level enforced. Attack vector: send nested table structure Table{Table{Table{...}}} 10,000+ levels deep.

claims.title: Wire-protocol length drives heap allocation without maximum bound (readBytes)
claims.impact: Denial of Service via heap exhaustion. An attacker controlling the AMQP connection (malicious server or MITM) can transmit a single frame with a `readBytes` length field set to a large value like 0x7FFFFFFE (2147483646), causing the client to attempt a multi-gigabyte heap allocation. If the allocation succeeds, it exhausts available heap; if rejected by the JVM, it crashes the client. Either way, further operations on that connection fail.
claims.evidence: Lines 86-88: `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()); if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE) { final byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength];` The condition at line 87 acts as a cast-safety guard (prevents overflow during int conversion) but not as a resource limit. It permits allocations up to 2147483646 bytes (~2 GB) based on untrusted wire-protocol input. This matches the vulnerable pattern in WEB-26: 'a cast-safety test (len < Integer.MAX_VALUE, n >= 0) is not a limit.' The code allocates before validating that the promised bytes are actually available in the buffer.

claims.title: Integer overflow in timestamp multiplication
claims.impact: Incorrect timestamp representation, potential for time-based logic bypass or incorrect chronological ordering of events. The Date constructor will receive a negative or wrapped millisecond value, causing the timestamp to represent an incorrect date (potentially in 1969 or other erroneous year). This could bypass time-based security checks or cause confusion in logging and audit trails.
claims.evidence: readTimestamp() (line 266-270) reads an 8-byte long value from the stream via in.readLong() and multiplies it by 1000 without overflow checking: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. If the input value is Long.MAX_VALUE (9,223,372,036,854,775,807), the multiplication overflows to a negative number due to Java's signed long wraparound.

claims.title: Unbounded memory allocation in protocol message parsing
claims.impact: Attacker sending a crafted AMQP message with a large byte-string field can cause out-of-memory condition, crashing the JVM and denying service to the application using this library.
claims.evidence: Method readBytes() allocates a byte array with size read directly from untrusted protocol input. Line 88: `byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength];` where contentLength is read from DataInputStream at line 86 and can be up to Integer.MAX_VALUE-1 (2,147,483,646 bytes = ~2 GB).

claims.title: Timestamp multiplication overflow in readTimestamp() — informational only
claims.impact: Integer overflow causes Date to be constructed with incorrect timestamp. However, since the timestamp value itself is attacker-controlled, this grants no capability beyond what the attacker already had (ability to send any timestamp).
claims.evidence: Method readTimestamp() multiplies long value by 1000 without overflow check: return new Date(in.readLong()*1000). When in.readLong() value exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 (~9.2 billion), multiplication overflows to incorrect value.

claims.title: Unbounded memory allocation via readBytes length prefix
claims.impact: An attacker sending a single AMQP frame with a large length-prefixed field (e.g., 2GB) forces the JVM to allocate contiguous memory, causing denial of service through heap exhaustion. The application will throw OutOfMemoryError and may crash.
claims.evidence: Lines 86-94: The readBytes() method reads a 32-bit unsigned integer from the stream as contentLength, then allocates a byte array of size (int)contentLength. The check `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` permits allocation of up to Integer.MAX_VALUE-1 bytes (approximately 2GB). This allocation is triggered whenever tables or long strings with large size fields are parsed: lines 103 (readLongstr), 147 (readTable), 241 (readArray).

claims.title: Unbounded memory allocation in readBytes() allows denial of service
claims.impact: Denial of service via heap exhaustion. Attacker can send crafted AMQP message with contentLength=Integer.MAX_VALUE-1, causing allocation of 2GB heap memory. Multiple requests exhaust available memory and crash JVM with OutOfMemoryError.
claims.evidence: Method readBytes() allocates byte array of size (int)contentLength without reasonable limit. contentLength is read as unsigned int from attacker-controlled stream via unsignedExtend(in.readInt()), allowing values up to Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 (2,147,483,647). Line 87-88 allocates: new byte[(int)contentLength].

claims.title: Uncontrolled memory allocation from wire protocol input
claims.impact: An attacker who can send AMQP messages (rogue server, MITM, or compromised broker) can cause denial of service by sending messages with extremely large size parameters. This will cause OutOfMemoryError when the client attempts to allocate huge byte arrays or read massive amounts of data into memory, crashing the application.
claims.evidence: readBytes method at line 86: `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` reads untrusted 32-bit length. Line 88 allocates: `new byte[(int)contentLength]` without size validation beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE check (2.1 GB). Similar pattern in readArray (line 240) and readTable (line 142) which read 32-bit length parameters and use them to create TruncatedInputStream.

claims.title: Stack overflow from unbounded recursion in field/table/array parsing
claims.impact: Denial of service through stack overflow. An attacker can craft an AMQP message with deeply nested table and array structures (e.g., a table containing an array containing a table containing an array, etc.) that trigger recursive calls. Each recursion consumes stack frames until StackOverflowError is thrown, crashing the thread or the entire JVM.
claims.evidence: readFieldValue() (line 158-221) recursively calls itself indirectly through: (1) case 'F' → readTable() (line 181), which calls readFieldValue() in a loop (line 150), and (2) case 'A' → readArray() (line 184), which calls readFieldValue() in a loop (line 245). There is no recursion depth limit or stack depth check anywhere in this chain.

claims.title: Unbounded recursion in table and array parsing
claims.impact: Attacker can cause denial of service by sending an AMQP message with a deeply nested table or array structure. This triggers unbounded recursion leading to StackOverflowError (crash) or memory exhaustion if the nesting is combined with large data at each level.
claims.evidence: Method readFieldValue() recursively calls itself indirectly through readTable() and readArray(). Case 'F' (lines 180-181) calls readTable() which calls readFieldValue() for each table entry. Case 'A' (lines 183-184) calls readArray() which calls readFieldValue() for each array element. No nesting depth limit or recursion check is implemented. A table containing a table containing a table... (arbitrarily deep) will recurse without bounds.

claims.title: Unbounded recursion in nested table and array deserialization
claims.impact: Stack overflow causing denial of service. A maliciously crafted AMQP message with deeply nested structures (e.g., table containing table containing table... repeated hundreds of times) exhausts the JVM call stack, triggering StackOverflowError and crashing the message handler or entire application.
claims.evidence: readFieldValue() at line 158 calls readTable() (line 181) or readArray() (line 184) in switch branches. readTable() at line 139 and readArray() at line 237 both invoke readFieldValue() in a loop (lines 150, 245). This forms an unbounded mutual recursion with no depth counter or limit. A message containing nested tables (type 'F') or arrays (type 'A') can recurse arbitrarily deep.

claims.title: Unbounded recursion depth in nested field structures (readFieldValue mutual recursion)
claims.impact: Denial of Service via stack exhaustion. An attacker can construct an AMQP frame with deeply nested tables or arrays, triggering StackOverflowError after roughly 10,000-50,000 levels of nesting (depending on stack frame size and JVM). The error crashes the client.
claims.evidence: Method readFieldValue() (lines 158-221) contains a switch statement that handles type discriminators. For type 'F' (line 180-181), it calls `readTable(in)`, which calls `readFieldValue()` in a loop (line 150). For type 'A' (line 183-184), it calls `readArray(in)`, which calls `readFieldValue()` in a loop (line 245). These form mutual recursion: `readFieldValue` → `readTable` → `readFieldValue` and `readFieldValue` → `readArray` → `readFieldValue`. No recursion depth parameter is threaded through these methods, so an attacker can nest arbitrarily deep: a table containing a field that is a table containing a field that is a table, etc. Each recursion level consumes stack space; depth N costs O(N) bytes of stack.

claims.title: Integer overflow in timestamp multiplication allows arbitrary Date construction
claims.impact: An attacker sending a crafted AMQP frame with a malformed timestamp field can cause integer overflow in the millisecond calculation, resulting in an incorrect Date object. This could affect timestamp-dependent logic such as message expiration checks, TTL validation, or audit log timestamps.
claims.evidence: Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);` reads an untrusted 64-bit timestamp from the AMQP protocol stream and multiplies by 1000 without overflow checking. When the timestamp value exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE / 1000 (9,223,372,036,854,775), the multiplication wraps around, producing an incorrect Date object.

claims.title: Reliance on InputStream.available() may cause premature loop termination and incomplete table/array parsing
claims.impact: If a table or array field is truncated mid-parse due to available() returning 0, the loop exits without consuming all the intended data. Subsequent reads from the stream would start at an incorrect position, causing protocol deserialization failure. This could be exploited as a denial-of-service vector if an attacker crafts a frame designed to trigger premature loop termination.
claims.evidence: Lines 148 and 244 use `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` and `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)` to control loop termination. The Java InputStream contract (Javadoc) states that available() returns 'an estimate' and may return 0 even when more data is available. If TruncatedInputStream's available() implementation is unreliable or if the wrapped stream does not accurately report available bytes, the loop may exit prematurely.

claims.title: Stack overflow from uncontrolled recursion in deserialization
claims.impact: An attacker can craft AMQP messages with deeply nested tables or arrays. When the client deserializes such a message, the stack will overflow, causing StackOverflowError and immediate application crash. This is a denial of service vulnerability.
claims.evidence: readFieldValue method (lines 158-221) recursively calls itself through readTable (line 181) and readArray (line 184). The cases for 'F' (table) and 'A' (array) dispatch to readTable and readArray respectively, which call readFieldValue in a loop. readTable at line 150 calls readFieldValue, and readArray at line 245 calls readFieldValue. No recursion depth counter or limit is present. Stack depth is unbounded based on message nesting level.

claims.title: Stack exhaustion via unbounded recursion in field value parsing
claims.impact: An attacker sending a frame with deeply nested AMQP table or array structures (e.g., a table containing a table containing a table, repeated N levels deep) will cause a StackOverflowError, crashing the consumer application.
claims.evidence: The readFieldValue() method (lines 158-221) is called recursively: case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable() which calls readFieldValue() again; case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray() which calls readFieldValue() again. No recursion depth limit is enforced in the code. A deeply nested table-of-tables or array-of-arrays can exhaust the call stack.

claims.title: Unbounded memory allocation from attacker-controlled content length
claims.impact: Denial of service through memory exhaustion. An attacker controlling the AMQP wire protocol data can trigger allocation of large byte arrays (up to 2GB each) from within readBytes() calls nested in readTable(), readArray(), and readFieldValue(). Multiple fields in a single message could allocate multiple 2GB+ arrays, exhausting heap memory and crashing the JVM.
claims.evidence: readBytes() at line 83-95 reads a 32-bit length prefix from untrusted network input via in.readInt(), sign-extends it to a long via unsignedExtend(), and allocates a byte array of that size. Line 87 checks `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` before allocation, permitting allocations up to 2,147,483,647 bytes (~2GB) per invocation.
